subject: Critical Thinking
title: Bayesian Thinking: Updating Beliefs with Evidence
description: A quick, practical guide to Bayesian Thinking: Updating Beliefs with Evidence.

hook.text: You're 80% sure it will rain. Then you see a blue sky. How should your confidence change? Bayes has the math.

buildup.text: Bayesian thinking: start with a prior belief, encounter new evidence, update proportionally. Never all-or-nothing.

discovery.text: Most people flip between 100% certain and 0%. Bayesians adjust gradually — each piece of evidence shifts the dial.

twist.text: Superforecasters — the best predictors in the world — are all Bayesian thinkers. They update often and by small amounts.

climax.text: The key habit: when encountering new information, ask 'How much should this change my confidence?'

punchline.text: Strong opinions, loosely held. Update constantly.

quiz.question: What is the core principle of Bayesian thinking?
options: Believe the first evidence you see
Update beliefs proportionally with each new piece of evidence

details.summary: Bayesian thinking means updating your beliefs proportionally when new evidence arrives rather than clinging to your original position or flipping entirely. It treats beliefs as probabilities that shift incrementally.
details.whyItMatters: Bayesian thinking is the gold standard for rational belief updating. It prevents both stubbornness and gullibility by calibrating belief changes to evidence strength.
takeaways: Start with a prior probability and update with new evidence
Strong evidence shifts beliefs more than weak evidence
Bayesian thinking prevents all-or-nothing belief changes

faq.question: How does Bayesian thinking differ from simply changing your mind?
faq.answer: Bayesian thinking changes your mind proportionally to evidence strength. A single anecdote should shift beliefs slightly; a rigorous study should shift them more. Simple mind-changing often overweights dramatic new information.

faq.question: What is a practical way to apply Bayesian thinking in daily life?
faq.answer: Before evaluating new evidence, estimate your current confidence as a percentage. After seeing the evidence, ask how much it should shift that number. This prevents emotional overreaction to single data points.
